analysis.one_liner: Lets homeowners facing foreclosure on modest homes stay in them as paying renters for five years.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote: it sat in the House Financial Services Committee from the day it was introduced in February 2016 until that Congress ended in January 2017.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would give homeowners whose modest homes are being foreclosed the option to keep living there as month-to-month renters, paying fair market rent set by a court, for up to five years. Foreclosure itself would still go forward and the lender could still sell the home, but the buyer could not evict the former owner during the five years if rent was paid on time. The bill applied to foreclosures already underway when it passed and to new ones started in the following five years, and it directed HUD to help homeowners use the right and report on how it was used.
analysis.who_benefits: Homeowners in foreclosure on below-median-priced, owner-occupied single-family homes with mortgages originated on or before the end of 2008 — largely families still caught in the aftermath of the housing crash. They would lose ownership of the home but keep a roof over their heads for up to five years at a rent a court sets at market rate, avoiding an abrupt eviction while they find new housing [S2][S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Homeowners facing foreclosure on modest homes

how_it_helps.text: An eligible homeowner — someone who lived in the home at least two years, bought it below the local median price, and took out the mortgage on or before December 31, 2008 — could choose to stay in the foreclosed home as a renter for five years, paying fair market rent [S3].
Foreclosure itself is not delayed or blocked: the bill explicitly preserves the creditor's right to foreclose and sell the property; only possession is subject to the five-year tenancy [S3].

Before any foreclosure could start, the lender would have to give written notice stating the default and telling the homeowner about the right to rent, with a waiting period before foreclosure could begin [S3].
Rent would be set by a court at fair market value, adjusted annually to changes in the housing component of the Consumer Price Index, with both sides able to ask for a redetermination [S3].
HUD would monitor compliance, help homeowners exercise the right, do outreach so people knew about it, and report to Congress yearly on how it was working [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Mortgage lenders, servicers, and investors who buy foreclosed properties. They would still recover the home through foreclosure and could sell it, but they could not take possession for up to five years while the former owner paid court-set market rent — tying up the property and delaying any resale or redevelopment [S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: Lenders and buyers of foreclosed homes

drawbacks.text: The bill does not save anyone's ownership: homeowners still lose the house to foreclosure and still owe whatever the mortgage contract requires; the bill only buys time as a renter [S3].

It ties up foreclosed properties for up to five years, which lenders and investors said would complicate recovering the value of their collateral and could raise the cost or availability of mortgage credit [S3].
Rent and disputes would be set through court proceedings, with an option to move the case to federal court, adding litigation for both homeowners and property owners [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the families it covered, the trade was clear: lose the title but keep the home for five years at a market rent, which is a substantial protection against sudden eviction. The cost falls on lenders and foreclosed-home buyers in the form of delayed possession, and critics could fairly argue that a broad, open-ended right to rent would chill lending; this version limited the exposure by covering only below-median-priced homes with pre-2009 mortgages and sunsetting after five years.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Financial Services Committee on the day it was introduced, and the committee never held a hearing or markup, so it died there when the 114th Congress ended in January 2017 [S1][S5].

narrative.text: Rep. Raúl Grijalva introduced the Right to Rent Act of 2016 on February 25, 2016 [S1][S5].
Ten Democratic colleagues cosponsored it; no Republicans did [S4].
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Financial Services the same day, which was its only action besides introduction [S5].
The committee took no further action, and the bill never reached the House floor before the 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017 [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Mortgage lenders, servicers, and investors in foreclosed homes — they kept the ability to take possession of foreclosed properties immediately, and foreclosed homeowners got no protection.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all ten cosponsors were Democrats and no Republicans signed on, and the Republican-controlled committee and floor schedule left the bill untouched.

industries.industry: Mortgage lenders, servicers, and investors in foreclosed homes
industries.note: The bill would have delayed their possession of foreclosed properties for up to five years while the former owner paid court-set market rent. Their interest in quick repossession and resale ran against homeowners' interest in staying housed, though they would still have received rent and kept the right to foreclose and sell.
Families in foreclosure on modest, owner-occupied homes would have gained up to five years of guaranteed occupancy at market rent, cushioning the blow of losing their home.
